Evidence · Canada

Built to Canada's Responsible Data Centre Development Principles

On 3 September 2026 the Government of Canada and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities published five principles for data centre development, and 23 companies signed. Two of the five ask for measurement. This page says what we measure, where, and who signs, on every project we deliver in Canada.

The two principles that ask for numbers

Principle 3. Data centres must minimize water use and environmental impacts, prioritizing "closed-loop or high efficiency water technologies, waste heat recovery, and low-emission energy sources," with water consumption and environmental impacts "measured and transparently reported using recognized standards."

Principle 4. Data centres must be transparent about local impacts, providing "clear, project-appropriate and independently verifiable information on expected local impacts, including power and water use, infrastructure requirements, sound and emissions."

The principles are voluntary and are addressed to developers and operators. We are a supplier. Our part is to make the numbers exist. Source: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada.

What we hand over, per site, per year

Electricity
  • IT load and facility overhead at the point of connection
  • Metering boundary drawn on a single-line diagram
  • PUE measured over the year at that boundary, not designed on paper
  • Connection and upgrade costs, and who paid each line
Water
  • Litres withdrawn and consumed, by source
  • WUE in litres per kWh of IT, measured, with the year stated
  • For closed loops: make-up volume and peak-day withdrawal
  • Days per year any evaporative assist runs, and the electricity dry cooling uses instead
Heat
  • MW available at the site boundary, and at what temperature
  • MWh actually delivered to a named receiver, metered at the boundary
  • What happens to the heat in months the receiver cannot take it
  • Zero is an honest number where no receiver exists yet, and we say so
Method
  • Who measured, at what load, in what period
  • Which standard: ISO/IEC 30134 for PUE, WUE and ERF
  • Who signed: on our projects, the commissioning agent
  • Where the record lives: in the turnover package, indexed by boundary

Why a supplier publishes this

Municipalities are being asked to assess projects against the principles. Most have no sheet to read. We published one, for any proponent to use, and we hold ourselves to it on every project. A council, a utility or a heat receiver should be able to answer the four questions above from our records without us in the room.

Guide for municipal staff. Reading a Data Centre's Power, Water and Heat Numbers: four pages, with a fourteen-line evidence schedule. Free to copy and adapt.

Questions this page answers

What do Canada's Responsible Data Centre Development Principles require on water and heat?

Principle 3 asks projects to prioritize closed-loop or high-efficiency water technologies, waste heat recovery and low-emission energy, and to measure and report water use and environmental impacts to recognized standards. Principle 4 asks for independently verifiable information on local impacts, including power and water use. The principles are voluntary; 23 companies signed on 3 September 2026. What our turnover package records →

How can a municipality verify a data centre's water and heat claims?

Ask for measured values at a stated boundary, not design values: annual water withdrawn and consumed, WUE in litres per kWh of IT, heat delivered in MWh to a named receiver, and PUE over the year, each signed by a party independent of the proponent. Write the list into the development agreement so every proponent answers the same questions. Who signs, and when →

Does closed-loop cooling mean a data centre uses no water?

No. Closed loops still take make-up water for leaks, sampling and fluid replacement, and some designs add evaporative assist on the hottest days. Ask for make-up volume, peak-day withdrawal and the days per year any evaporative assist runs, and ask for the electricity that dry cooling uses instead of water. Why the loop temperature matters →

We do not manufacture components. We take responsibility for the whole thermal path, and we hand over the evidence.
